# I need to report rats in my building

Description: File a complaint about rats through SF 311. The city will inspect and require your landlord to fix the problem.

## What to know before you start

Before calling 311, tell your landlord about the problem in writing. Wait 72 hours for them to respond. If they do not fix the problem, then contact 311.

Cost: Free

Things to know:
- You must give written notice to your landlord first
- The inspector will need access to your unit
- Rats are a serious health hazard that landlords must fix
- The city can fine landlords who do not fix rat problems

## What to do

Section heading: Call 311 to file a complaint
Section body: Call 311 or go to sf.gov/311 to report rats in your building.

311 will ask you:
- Your name and contact information
- Your address
- Details about where you see rats
- When you notified your landlord
- If you can give the inspector access to your unit

All complaints start with 311. 311 takes your complaint and your details. If the case fits HHVC rules, 311 sends it to HHVC.

Section heading: What 311 does with your complaint
Section body: SF 311 forwards your complaint to the Department of Public Health. An inspector will contact you within 5 business days to schedule an inspection.

The inspector will visit your building to look for signs of rats and check if your landlord is following housing laws.

Section heading: Signs of rats to report
Section body: Tell 311 if you see any of these signs:
- Rat droppings (small, dark pellets)
- Dead rats
- Rat holes or gnaw marks
- Rats running around your unit or building
- Food containers chewed open
- Strange smells or sounds in walls

Section heading: What happens next
Section body: After you call 311, an inspector will contact you to schedule a visit. If the inspector finds violations, your landlord gets a notice to fix the problems. You will get updates through 311. Keep your case number to track progress.

Phone number: 311

# I need to fix mold in my rental

Description: Report mold problems in your rental unit and learn what you and your landlord are responsible for fixing.

## What to know before you start

The San Francisco Department of Public Health can help when mold covers 10 or more square feet on walls and ceilings. We cannot help with mold on personal belongings like furniture or clothes.

Mold comes from two main sources. Leaks are your landlord's responsibility to fix. Condensation from daily activities like cooking and showering is your responsibility to control.

## What to do

Section heading: Call 311 to report the problem
Section body: Call 311 or go to sf.gov/311 to report mold in your rental. You will need to provide your address and describe where you see the mold.

A health inspector will schedule a time to visit your unit. You must give the inspector access to your rental.

The inspector will measure the moldy area and determine if your landlord must clean it and paint with mold-resistant paint.

Section heading: Before you call 311
Section body: Wait 72 hours after notifying your landlord in writing about the mold problem. Keep a copy of your written notice.

Take photos of the moldy areas to show the inspector.

Section heading: Landlord responsibilities
Section body:
- Fix any leaks in plumbing, roof, or windows
- Clean mold covering 10 or more square feet on walls and ceilings
- Paint with mold-resistant paint after cleaning
- Allow inspector access to make repairs

Section heading: Tenant responsibilities
Section body:
- Control humidity inside your unit
- Keep your home clean and uncluttered
- Store food properly
- Notify your landlord in writing about leaks
- Give access for inspections and repairs
- Use exhaust fans when cooking and showering
- Open windows daily to air out your home

Section heading: Prevent mold from coming back
Section body: Keep humidity below 55 percent. Run exhaust fans for 15 to 20 minutes after cooking or showering. Keep air moving with fans when you are home. Pull furniture at least 6 inches away from exterior walls. Wipe up condensation on windows and sills right away.

Section heading: What happens next
Section body: After you call 311, an inspector will contact you within 5 business days. If the inspector finds a violation, your landlord will get a notice to fix the problem.

Phone number: 311

# I need to report mold in my home

Description: Report mold problems in your rental unit and learn what your landlord must do to fix them.

## What to know before you start

Cost: Free

Things to know: Write to your landlord first. Wait 72 hours before calling the City. We check your unit for mold and can order your landlord to fix it. We look at mold that covers 10 square feet or more.

## What to do

Section heading: Find out what causes the mold
Section body: Look for water leaks. Check pipes, windows, and the roof. Look for wet spots on walls. If you see leaks, your landlord must fix them. If the mold comes from humidity in your unit, you need to control moisture. Open windows and use fans.

Section heading: Write to your landlord
Section body: Write a letter about the mold. Tell your landlord the date you found it. Tell them where the mold is. Ask them to fix the mold and any leaks. Keep a copy of your letter. Wait 72 hours for them to answer.

Section heading: Call the City
Section body: Call 311 if your landlord does not fix the mold in 72 hours. Tell 311 you want to report mold in your rental. Give them your address. Tell them about the mold problem. All complaints start with 311. 311 takes your complaint and your details. If the case fits HHVC rules, 311 sends it to HHVC.

Action link: Report mold through SF311 [https://sf.gov/report-request-or-complaint]

Phone number: 311

Section heading: What happens next
Section body: A housing inspector will visit your unit. You must be home for the visit or let your landlord give access. The inspector will look for mold, leaks, and air flow problems. If they find problems, your landlord gets a notice to fix them.

Callout: We check mold that covers 10 square feet or more on walls or ceilings. You must let the City inspector into your unit and let your landlord in to make repairs. Your responsibilities include controlling humidity in your unit by opening windows and using fans, keeping your unit clean, writing to your landlord first and waiting 72 hours before calling the City.

# I need to report bedbugs in my home

Description: Report bedbug problems in your San Francisco home through 311 and learn your responsibilities as a tenant.

## What to know before you start

Section heading: When to report bedbugs
Section body: You should report bedbugs to the city if your landlord has not fixed the problem within 72 hours of your written notice. Bedbugs are small, brown insects that feed on blood and leave red, itchy bites. You might see dark spots on your mattress, sheets, or furniture. You might also notice a sweet, musty smell.

Section heading: What happens after you report
Section body: The city will create a case number for your report. An inspector will contact you within 5 business days to schedule an inspection. You must provide access to your unit during normal business hours. The inspector will check for bedbugs and write a report. If bedbugs are found, the city will order your landlord to fix the problem.

Callout: You must write to your landlord first and wait 72 hours before reporting to the city. Keep a copy of your written notice.

## What to do

Section heading: Before you report
Section body: Write a letter or email to your landlord describing the bedbug problem. Include the date you first noticed bedbugs. Keep a copy for your records. Wait 72 hours after sending your notice before contacting 311.

Section heading: Report to 311
Section body: Call 311 or use the SF311 app to report bedbugs. You can also submit a report online at sf.gov/311. Tell them you need to report bedbugs in your rental unit. Give them your address and explain what you have seen or experienced. All complaints start with 311. 311 gives you a case number. If the case fits HHVC rules, 311 sends it to HHVC. Write down your case number.

Button link: Report online to 311 [sf.gov/311]

Phone number: 311

Section heading: What you need to do
Section body: Clean and organize your unit before the inspection. Remove clutter from floors and surfaces. Wash and dry all bedding and clothes on high heat if possible. Vacuum carpets and furniture. You must be available during normal business hours to let the inspector into your unit.

Callout: Tenant responsibilities: You are responsible for controlling humidity inside your unit, keeping your unit clean, writing to your landlord first and waiting 72 hours before contacting the city, and providing access for inspection and repairs.

# I need help with housing health and pest problems

Description: Report pests, request inspections, and get housing health help from San Francisco's Healthy Housing and Vector Control team.

## Overview

Text: You have the right to safe, healthy housing in San Francisco. The Healthy Housing and Vector Control team helps with pest problems, housing conditions, and health hazards in homes and apartments.

We handle complaints about cockroaches, rodents, bed bugs, and other pests. We also inspect housing conditions that affect your health and safety. This includes residential hotels and SROs.

Most services start with a call to 311. Our team will follow up within 5 business days after report is received from 311. For bed bugs and sewage problems, we will respond within 48 hours.

## Contact us

Phone number: (415) 252-3800

Address: San Francisco Department of Public Health, Healthy Housing and Vector Control, 1380 Howard Street 2nd Floor, San Francisco CA 94103

Text: Office hours: Monday through Friday, 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM. For emergencies outside business hours, call 311.

## What to do

Button link: Start a report [Link to HHVC inspection request form]

Section heading: What we inspect
Section body: We inspect rental homes for health problems that your landlord must fix. This includes rats, roaches, bed bugs, cockroaches, mold, leaks, sewage backups, broken plumbing, poor ventilation, and trash buildup. We check if your home meets San Francisco housing health standards.

Section heading: What happens during an inspection
Section body: Fill out our inspection request form to tell us about the health problem in your home. An inspector will visit your building within 5 business days after report is received from 311 to check the problem.

Our inspector will look at the problem areas you reported. Leave any evidence of pests or damage in place so the inspector can document it. Do not clean up pest droppings or throw away damaged items before the inspection. The inspector will take notes and measurements to create an official report.

If we find violations, your landlord will get a notice to fix them. You do not pay anything for this service.

Section heading: Your responsibilities
Section body: You must control humidity inside your unit, keep your unit clean, store food properly, and give the inspector access to your home. You also must write to your landlord about the problem before contacting us.

# I need help with mold and water

Description: Easy steps to follow if you have leaks or damp walls in your home.

## What to do

Section heading: Call 311 if your landlord won't fix leaks or mold
Section body: You must write to your landlord first about any leak or mold problem. Keep a copy of your letter. If your landlord does not fix the problem within 72 hours, call 311 to report it.

Action link: Call 311

Section heading: Signs that need your landlord's attention
Section body:
- Any water leak from pipes, water heater, roof, windows, or doors
- Dark spots or patches on walls or ceiling
- Water stains or peeling paint
- Damp areas that won't dry
- Musty smells
- Mold covering 10 square feet or more on walls and ceilings

Section heading: What happens when you call 311
Section body: An inspector will visit your home within 5 business days after report is received from 311. The inspector will look at the mold and water damage. If we find violations, your landlord will get a notice to fix the problem. Leave any mold or water damage visible so our inspector can see it and measure it.

Callout: We can only help with mold on walls and ceilings that covers 10 square feet or more. We cannot help with mold on your personal belongings like furniture, clothing, or household items.

Section heading: What your landlord must fix
Section body: Your landlord must fix all leaks. This includes dripping pipes, water heater leaks, roof leaks, and leaks around windows or doors. Your landlord must also clean mold that covers 10 square feet or more on walls and ceilings.

Section heading: What you control
Section body: You control humidity inside your unit. This means managing moisture from cooking, showering, and everyday living. You also keep your unit clean and wipe up condensation on windows.

Callout: You must write to your landlord first about leaks and wait 72 hours before contacting the city. You must also give your landlord access to make repairs and control humidity in your unit.

Section heading: Daily steps to control moisture
Section body:
- Open windows for 5 to 15 minutes every day
- Run exhaust fans when cooking or showering and for 15 minutes after
- Use a fan to keep air moving in your home
- Keep furniture 6 inches away from outside walls
- Wipe up water on windows and sills right away
- Cover pots and pans when cooking
- Keep humidity below 55 percent if you have a device to measure it

Section heading: How to clean small amounts of mold
Section body: Use soap and water to clean small mold spots. Do not use bleach. Wash moldy clothes in warm water and dry them completely. If you have an air purifier with a HEPA filter, it can help capture mold spores in the air.

Phone number: 311

# I need help with trash and messes

Description: Easy steps to follow if you have garbage, sewage, or waste problems.

## What to do

Section heading: Call 311 right away for urgent problems
Section body: Call 311 immediately if you have:
- Raw sewage in your unit
- Blocked drains causing flooding
- Garbage that attracts pests
- Waste problems that smell bad or make you sick

We will send an inspector to check your home within 48 hours for sewage problems.

Action link: Call 311

Callout: Sewage reports receive a response within 48 hours.

Section heading: For other trash problems, try this first
Section body: Many trash problems can be solved between you and your landlord:
1. Write to your landlord about the problem
2. Keep a copy of your letter
3. Wait 72 hours for your landlord to respond
4. If nothing improves, call 311

Section heading: Trash and waste problems we handle
Section body: We help with health and safety problems caused by trash and waste in your home or building:
- Sewage backups in your unit or building
- Blocked drains that cause health problems
- Garbage piling up because your landlord won't provide trash service
- Waste that attracts pests like rats or roaches
- Broken plumbing that affects your health

Callout: We handle health problems from trash and waste. For broken pipes or plumbing repairs, contact the Department of Building Inspection (DBI).

Section heading: What you need to do
Section body: You are responsible for:
- Keeping your own unit clean
- Taking your trash to the building's garbage area
- Not blocking drains with grease or large items
- Writing to your landlord about problems first

Section heading: What your landlord must do
Section body: Your landlord is responsible for:
- Providing trash service for the building
- Fixing sewage problems within 48 hours
- Keeping shared areas like hallways and basements clean
- Making sure plumbing works properly
- Removing pest-attracting waste from the property

Description: Report overgrown plants and weeds that create pest problems or block access to your building.

## What to do

Section heading: Before you call 311
Section body: Try these steps first to solve the problem on your own:
- Talk to your landlord or property manager about trimming overgrown plants
- Write a letter to your property owner if talking does not work
- Wait 72 hours after writing to your landlord before contacting the city

Section heading: Report the problem
Section body: Call 311 to report overgrown vegetation at your building. Have this information ready when you call:
- Your address and the problem location
- When you contacted your landlord about the problem
- Whether the vegetation is blocking access or attracting pests

Action link: Report plants and weeds online [Link to 311 online reporting system]

Phone number: 311

Section heading: What happens next
Section body: After you report the problem:
- An inspector will visit the property within 5 business days after report is received from 311
- The inspector will check if the vegetation violates health and safety rules
- If there is a violation, the property owner gets a notice to fix the problem
- You will get a letter with the inspection results

Section heading: What we inspect for
Section body: We check for vegetation problems that affect health and safety:
- Tall weeds or grass that hide rats and other pests
- Overgrown bushes that block building entrances or fire exits
- Dead plants that create fire hazards
- Vegetation that prevents access for inspections or repairs
- Plants growing too close to buildings and causing moisture problems

Callout: We do not handle tree removal, sidewalk weeds, or plants on city property. Contact the Department of Public Works at 311 for those issues. The property owner is responsible for maintaining their yard and landscaping. Tenants should notify their landlord first before contacting the city.

# I need to pay my annual building fee

Description: Owners of buildings with 3 or more apartments must pay this fee every year.

## Pay your fee

Section heading: Pay online
Section body: The fastest way to pay is online. You will need your account number from your bill.

Button link: Pay your fee online [URL to be confirmed with HHVC]

Section heading: Pay by phone or in person
Section body: Call 311 to pay by phone or get our office address to pay in person.

Phone number: 311

Callout: Keep your payment receipt. You may need it during your building inspection.

Section heading: Who must pay
Section body: You must pay this fee if you own a building with 3 or more apartments in San Francisco. This includes condos, flats, and rental units. Buildings with 1 or 2 units do not need to pay this fee.

Section heading: Payment deadlines
Section body: You must pay this fee every year by the deadline. The city sends you a bill in the mail with your payment due date. If you do not pay on time, you will owe late fees. We cannot inspect your building until you pay the fee.

Section heading: Fee amounts
Section body: The fee amount depends on how many units are in your building. More units cost more. Check your bill or call 311 for your exact fee amount. The fee covers our health and safety inspections of your building.

Callout: This fee is separate from building permits or other city fees. It only covers health inspections by HHVC.

# I need to fix a violation after an inspection

Description: What to do after you get a notice from an HHVC inspection.

## What to do

Section heading: Contact your investigator first
Section body: Your violation notice has the name and contact information of the HHVC investigator who did your inspection. Contact them directly to:
- Ask questions about the violation
- Understand what repairs you need to make
- Request a re-inspection after you fix the problem

Section heading: Steps to fix your violation
Section body: Follow these steps to fix your violation:
1. Read your notice carefully to understand what needs to be fixed
2. Contact licensed contractors or pest control professionals if needed
3. Keep receipts and take notes about the work you do
4. Do not remove or hide evidence of the problem before repairs are complete

Our inspectors need to see the original issue to verify your repairs.

Callout: Do not remove evidence of bugs, mold, or damage before making repairs. Leave it for our inspector to document.

Section heading: Standard repair timelines
Section body: Your notice shows how much time you have to make repairs:
- Emergency health hazards (sewage, bed bugs): 24 hours
- Routine maintenance issues: 30 days
- Other violations: time varies based on the specific problem

Contact your investigator if you need more time or have questions about your deadline.

Section heading: Why you got this notice
Section body: You received this notice because an HHVC inspector found a health problem in your building. You must fix these problems to keep your building safe and healthy for tenants.

Section heading: What happens if you do not fix it
Section body: If you do not fix the violations, you may face:
- Fines
- Legal action
- The City doing the work and billing you for costs

Button link: Prepare for your DPH Director's Hearing [Link to existing SF.gov Director's Hearing page]

Section heading: How to appeal a violation
Section body: If you believe the violation was issued in error, you can appeal:
1. Contact your investigator within 10 days to discuss your concerns
2. Request a Director's Hearing if you cannot resolve the issue directly
3. Attend the hearing to present your case

You must appeal quickly. Do not wait until the repair deadline has passed.

Section heading: HHVC vs. Building Inspection — who to contact
Section body: HHVC handles health and sanitation concerns: bugs, mold, sewage. The Department of Building Inspection (DBI) handles: structural issues, electrical problems, life-safety issues.

# My rules as a building owner

Description: Requirements for owners of buildings with 3 or more apartments.

## What to do

Section heading: Register your building and pay the annual fee
Section body: You must register your building with HHVC and pay an annual fee if you own a building with 3 or more apartments. This includes apartment buildings, condos, and mixed-use buildings. You must register every year, even if nothing has changed.

Action link: Call 311 to register or pay your fee

Section heading: Fix rat problems within 30 days
Section body: You must keep rats out of your building and fix any rat problems within 30 days of learning about them. This means sealing holes where rats can enter, keeping garbage areas clean, and working with tenants to eliminate food sources. You cannot pass these costs to tenants through rent increases.

Section heading: Building maintenance you must provide
Section body: You must provide working plumbing, heating, and ventilation in all units. You must keep common areas clean and store garbage in covered containers. You must make repairs within 30 days of getting a violation notice.

Section heading: How to work with your tenants
Section body: You need to tell tenants to store food properly and keep their units clean. Tenants must let you into their units for repairs and pest control. They must write to you about problems before calling the city.

Callout: You must give inspectors access to all parts of your building, including basements, storage areas, and vacant units.

Section heading: What inspectors look for
Section body: Inspectors look for rat signs like droppings, gnaw marks, and entry points. They check garbage storage, building maintenance, and common areas. You should leave any evidence you find so inspectors can see the problem.

Callout: Not sure who to contact? HHVC handles health problems like rats, mold, and sewage. The Department of Building Inspection handles structural problems, electrical work, and building permits.

Action link: Call 311 for questions or to report problems

- Environmental health risks in your area

# I need to report rats in my home

Description: Report rats when your landlord won't get rid of them. We inspect and make landlords fix rat problems in rental homes.

## What to know before you start

Section heading: Before you call 311
Section body: You must try to resolve the problem with your landlord first. Write to your landlord about the rats and keep a copy. Give your landlord 72 hours to respond or start fixing the problem. Leave evidence like rat droppings undisturbed for our inspector to document. Keep records of all communication with your landlord.

Section heading: What we look for during rat inspections
Section body: We can help when you have rats in your home. Our inspectors look for rat droppings, gnaw marks on food or furniture, nesting materials like shredded paper, holes where rats get in, and dead rats. We also check if your landlord is doing enough to keep rats out.

Callout: You are responsible for keeping your home clean, storing food in sealed containers, and giving access for inspections and repairs.

## What to do

Section heading: Start your report
Section body: Call 311 or report online. Tell them you have rats that your landlord won't fix. Give them your address and describe what you see. All complaints start with 311. 311 takes your complaint and your details. If the case fits HHVC rules, 311 sends it to HHVC.

Action link: Report rats online through 311 [sf.gov/311-customer-service-center]

Phone number: 311

Section heading: After you report
Section body: An inspector will contact you within 5 business days to schedule a visit. You must be available to let the inspector into your home. The inspector will also contact your landlord.

Section heading: During the inspection
Section body: The inspector will document any health code violations and give your landlord a written notice to get rid of the rats. Most repairs must be completed within 30 days.

Callout: Not sure who to contact? We handle health problems like rats. The Department of Building Inspection handles structural problems like broken walls or doors where rats might get in.

# I need to report flies in my home

Description: Get city help when flies in your home won't go away and your landlord won't fix the problem.

## What to do

Callout: You must notify your landlord in writing about the fly problem and wait 72 hours before contacting the city.

Section heading: Before you call the city
Section body: You write to your landlord about the fly problem. You keep a copy of your letter or email. You wait 72 hours after sending it. You leave evidence of the flies for the inspector to see during the visit.

Section heading: Report the problem
Section body: You call 311 or file a report online. You tell them you have flies in your home and your landlord will not fix the cause. You give your address and contact information. You mention if you see flies near garbage, drains, or broken pipes. All complaints start with 311. 311 takes your complaint and your details. If the case fits HHVC rules, 311 sends it to HHVC.

Button link: File a report online [sf.gov/report-request-non-emergency-services]

Action link: Call 311 now [tel:311]

Phone number: 311

Section heading: During the inspection
Section body: You give the inspector access to your home. You show them where you see the most flies. You point out any broken plumbing, garbage problems, or openings where flies might enter. The inspector will look for health code violations your landlord must fix.

Section heading: When we can help
Section body: We inspect for health violations when flies are caused by broken plumbing, garbage problems, or structural issues your landlord should fix. We cannot help with flies from normal household activities or cleanliness issues.

Section heading: What happens next
Section body: An inspector will visit within 5 business days after report is received from 311 to check for health code violations. If we find violations, your landlord must fix them or face fines. You do not pay for this service.

Callout — Your responsibilities:
- Controlling humidity inside your unit
- Keeping your unit clean
- Writing to your landlord first and waiting 72 hours before contacting the city

Section heading: Not sure who to contact?
Section body: The Department of Public Health handles health and sanitation concerns like flies from broken pipes or garbage. The Department of Building Inspection handles structural repairs like broken windows or doors.

# I need to report cockroaches in my home

Description: Get city help to eliminate cockroaches when your landlord won't fix the problem. Report through 311.

## What to do

Section heading: Call 311 to report
Section body: Call 311 and say you want to report cockroaches in your home. Give them your address and explain that you already contacted your landlord in writing. All complaints start with 311. 311 gives you a case number. If the case fits HHVC rules, 311 sends it to HHVC for review and inspection scheduling.

Action link: Call 311 now [Phone: 311]

Phone number: 311

Section heading: Before you call 311
Section body: You need to write to your landlord about the cockroaches first. You should keep a copy of what you wrote and wait 72 hours after writing to your landlord. If they do not respond or fix the problem, then you can call 311.

Section heading: Leave evidence for the inspector
Section body: You should not clean up all signs of cockroaches before the inspection. You need to leave some droppings, egg cases, or dead cockroaches so the inspector can document the problem. You should clean up food and water sources but leave evidence of the pests.

## What to know before you start

Section heading: When to contact the city
Section body: You can contact 311 if you told your landlord about cockroaches in writing and waited 72 hours but they still have not fixed the problem. You can also contact the city right away if cockroaches are in common areas like hallways or laundry rooms.

Section heading: What happens after you report
Section body: The city will inspect your building within 5 business days after report is received from 311. If they find cockroaches or conditions that attract them, they will order your landlord to fix the problem. Your landlord must eliminate the cockroaches and remove the conditions that let them survive.

Section heading: What to expect during inspection
Section body: The inspector will look for cockroaches and the conditions that let them survive. This includes checking for food sources, water leaks, cracks where they hide, and trash storage. You must give the inspector access to your unit and common areas.

Callout: You do not pay any fees to report cockroaches or get an inspection.

Callout: Your responsibilities: Control humidity in your unit, keep your unit clean, store food properly, write to your landlord first and wait 72 hours, give access for inspection and repairs.
